01.actor: Rabbi Tarfon, Rabbi Akiva and the Elders
01.event: While the sages were reclining in the upper room of the house of Nit'za in Lod, they were asked whether study or action is greater.
01.turn: Rabbi Tarfon said action is greater, but Rabbi Akiva said study is greater.
01.outcome: All of them agreed that study is greater, because study leads to action.
01.summary: Rabbi Tarfon and the Elders were gathered in an upper room in Lod when someone asked them whether study or action is greater. Rabbi Tarfon answered that action is greater; Rabbi Akiva answered that study is greater. In the end everyone agreed with Akiva, on the grounds that study leads to action.

02.event: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives, burdened with their father's widow's daily medical costs, asked him for advice, and he told them to fix a lump sum with the doctor.
02.turn: Rabbi Yohanan came to regret the advice, feeling he had acted like a legal advocate for his own family.
02.outcome: He concluded that a man of stature is different and should not help relatives in a way that harms another.
02.summary: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives had to pay for their father's widow, who needed treatment every day. They came to him for advice, and he told them to set a fixed fee with the doctor, which would shift the cost onto her marriage settlement. Afterward he regretted it, saying he had made himself like a lawyer, since an important person should not appear to favor his relatives.

04.actor: Ravina and Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak
04.event: Ravina found Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak leaning on a door bar, puzzling over a legal question.
04.summary: Ravina came upon Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak leaning on the bar of a door, deep in thought over whether a husband who simply says a divorce document is 'void' cancels it. No answer is recorded, and the question stands.
04.missing: Any interaction or development beyond the scene of the sage pondering.

05.event: Ben Nappaha owned houses in five courtyards in Usha, and his case came before the Sages.
05.outcome: The Sages ruled that only his place of residence restricts carrying.
05.summary: Ben Nappaha had houses in five courtyards in Usha, only one of which he lived in. The question of whether he restricted carrying in all of them came before the Sages, who ruled that only the place where he actually lived counted.
05.missing: Anything beyond a bare case and its ruling.

06.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, Rabbi Yishmael, Rabbi Yohanan, Rav Shemen bar Abba
06.event: Similar cases about a deserted wife's sustenance came before Rabbi in Beit She'arim and Rabbi Yishmael in Tzippori, who ruled differently.
06.turn: Rabbi Yohanan wondered at the ruling that denied her sustenance, and Rav Shemen bar Abba told him Shmuel had already explained it as a case where the husband was reported dead.
06.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan expressed astonishment at how far they had analyzed it.
06.summary: Two similar cases of a woman whose husband had gone abroad came before Rabbi and before Rabbi Yishmael, and one granted her sustenance while the other did not. Rabbi Yohanan was puzzled by the refusal. Rav Shemen bar Abba told him that Shmuel in Babylonia had explained it as a case where the husband was reported dead, and Rabbi Yohanan was amazed. A second version swaps which judge ruled which way.
06.missing: The facts of the cases themselves are only alluded to; the exchange is mostly legal interpretation.

07.actor: A man captured with his mother; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
07.event: A man casually remarked that he and his mother had been taken captive and that he had never stopped watching over her.
07.turn: Though a son cannot normally testify for his mother, his remark was unconsidered and incidental.
07.outcome: Rabbi permitted his mother to marry a priest on the basis of his words.
07.summary: A man chatting offhandedly said that he and his mother had been held captive among gentiles, and that whether drawing water or gathering wood his mind was always on his mother. Because he said it in passing rather than as testimony, Rabbi accepted it and allowed his mother to marry into the priesthood.

08.event: A man prepared a betrothal feast on the ninetieth day after the woman's husband died.
08.summary: A man arranged a betrothal feast on the ninetieth day after his bride's first husband had died, and Rava stopped it, so the feast went to waste. The Gemara then explains it was really a wedding feast, not a betrothal.
08.missing: Any detail beyond a one-line report used as a legal proof.

09.event: A man told Rabbi Ami that someone had a presumption of priesthood because he read first in the synagogue.
09.turn: Rabbi Ami questioned whether he read first as a priest or as a great man, and the witness showed a Levite read after him.
09.outcome: Rabbi Ami confirmed the man as a priest on his word.
09.summary: A man came to Rabbi Ami claiming that another was known to be a priest because he was called first to the Torah. Rabbi Ami pressed him: perhaps he was honored as a scholar, not as a priest. The witness answered that a Levite was called right after him, and Rabbi Ami accepted the man as a priest.

10.event: Rav Yosef said he had never heard a certain teaching.
10.turn: His student Abaye reminded him that Rav Yosef himself had taught it to them, and in what context.
10.summary: Rav Yosef said he had never heard a certain ruling. Abaye told him that he had in fact taught it to them himself, reconstructing the discussion in which he had cited it. The passage does not say how Rav Yosef responded.
10.missing: Rav Yosef's reaction; the cause of his forgetting is given only in the translator's gloss.

11.actor: Rav Avya and his wife, sister of Rami bar Hama
11.event: The sister of Rami bar Hama was married to Rav Avya, and her marriage contract was lost.
11.turn: They came before Rav Yosef, who cited a ruling that it is Rabbi Meir's view that living without a full marriage contract is forbidden.
11.summary: Rami bar Hama's sister was married to Rav Avya, and her marriage contract was lost. The couple went to Rav Yosef, who told them that the view that such a marriage is improper belongs to Rabbi Meir. The resolution is not shown.
11.missing: The passage itself is only the opening line; the rest of the story and its ending lie beyond the text shown.

12.event: Rav Kahana held beer belonging to the orphan Rav Mesharshiyya bar Hilkai and delayed selling it until the Festival.
12.outcome: He explained that even if it soured somewhat, it would fetch ready cash at the Festival.
12.summary: Rav Kahana was holding beer that belonged to an orphan and waited until the Festival to sell it. He explained that even if it went a little sour, it would sell for good cash then.
12.missing: No turn or result; it is an action with its rationale.

13.event: A person of indeterminate sex in Biri was operated on and the covering of his genitals torn open.
13.outcome: Rabbi Yehuda's view is defended by suggesting the children were not his.
13.summary: In the town of Biri there was a tumtum who was placed in a chair and surgically opened, and who went on to father seven children. Rabbi Ami cites this against Rabbi Yehuda, who could answer that the children's paternity should be checked.
13.missing: The case is only cited as an objection; it is not told as a narrative.

14.event: Minyamin, a first-generation Egyptian convert, married another first-generation Egyptian convert.
14.outcome: He planned to marry his son to a second-generation Egyptian convert so that his grandson could enter the congregation.
14.summary: Rabbi Yehuda recalled his friend Minyamin, an Egyptian convert among Rabbi Akiva's students. Minyamin said he had married a first-generation Egyptian convert and intended to marry his son to a second-generation one, so that his grandson would be permitted to marry into Israel.
14.missing: It is a reported statement of plans; the outcome is not told.

16.event: A debtor hid his money by claiming it belonged to a gentile.
16.turn: Because he acted improperly, the Sages acted harshly with him.
16.outcome: They forced him to sell his land to pay the creditor.
16.summary: Asked what really happened in a case attributed to Rava, Rav Hama explained that the debtor had shielded his money by claiming it was a gentile's. Because he behaved dishonestly, the Sages treated him harshly and made him sell his land himself to pay.
16.missing: The forced sale is supplied partly from context and the translator's gloss.

17.actor: Reish Lakish, Rabbi Elazar, Rabbi Yohanan
17.event: Reish Lakish demanded proof of threshing-floor teruma to confirm a priest, and Rabbi Elazar objected; later the same happened before Rabbi Yohanan, who raised the same objection.
17.turn: Reish Lakish realized Rabbi Elazar had been quoting Rabbi Yohanan without attribution.
17.outcome: Reish Lakish glared at Rabbi Elazar and rebuked him for not citing bar Nappaha by name.
17.summary: A man told Reish Lakish someone was a priest because he read first from the Torah; Reish Lakish asked whether he had seen him receive teruma, and Rabbi Elazar retorted that priesthood cannot depend on a threshing floor. Later, before Rabbi Yohanan, the same exchange happened and Rabbi Yohanan said the very same words. Reish Lakish turned and glared at Rabbi Elazar: you heard this from bar Nappaha and did not tell us in his name?

18.event: Rav Yosef said he had never heard a certain teaching.
18.turn: Abaye reminded him that he himself had taught it, and had even drawn three conclusions from it.
18.summary: Rav Yosef said he did not know a ruling about side posts. His student Abaye reminded him that he had taught them that very ruling and had derived three laws from it, which Abaye then listed. Rav Yosef's response is not given.
18.missing: Rav Yosef's reaction; the reason he forgot appears only in the translator's gloss.

19.actor: Residents of a crooked alley in Sura; Rav Hisda
19.event: Residents placed a rolled-up mat at the bend of a crooked alley to permit carrying.
19.turn: Rav Hisda declared it valid by neither Rav nor Shmuel.
19.outcome: The mat was deemed ineffective because the wind could blow it over.
19.summary: In Sura, the people of an L-shaped alley rolled up a mat and set it at the bend as a side post. Rav Hisda said this works by no one's opinion, since a mat the wind can knock down counts for nothing.
19.missing: Most of the passage is legal analysis; the event is a single action.

20.event: Rabbi Elazar taught that the unlearned will not be resurrected, and Rabbi Yohanan objected that God would not be pleased.
20.turn: Rabbi Elazar defended his view from another verse, then saw that Rabbi Yohanan was grieved.
20.outcome: Rabbi Elazar found a remedy: those who support Torah scholars are counted as cleaving to God.
20.summary: Rabbi Elazar taught that common, unlearned people will not rise at the resurrection. Rabbi Yohanan protested that God would not be pleased with such a statement, and Rabbi Elazar backed it with another verse. Seeing his teacher distressed, Rabbi Elazar told him he had found them a remedy: whoever marries his daughter to a scholar or supports scholars with his wealth is considered to cleave to the Divine Presence.
